About the Life Support Skills event

Life Support Skills is a Emergency Preparedness event in the HOSA secondary division. Format: skills · online submission. This event has special eligibility requirements, so check the guidelines with your advisor.

Ten step-by-step lessons for the solo HOSA Life Support Skills event, written in clear, plain language. You will be judged on one CPR skill (adult CPR, adult CPR with an AED or infant CPR) and one first aid skill (EpiPen, severe bleeding, choking, open fracture and splint, heat emergency, severe burn or naloxone). Each lesson follows the 2026–27 rating sheet in order, with practice tips, step-ordering drills, sorting games and short scenarios. Built around the American Heart Association and American Red Cross guidelines. Tell the judge which one you follow before you start.

Life Support Skills lessons

Unit 1 · Getting ready and adult CPR

Shared steps for every skill, Skill I (adult CPR) and Skill II (adult CPR with AED).

  1. Getting ready: the event and the steps every skill shares 30 min

    Life Support Skills teaches you to help someone in an emergency before an ambulance arrives. You will show a judge one CPR skill and one first aid skill. Many steps are the same in every skill. If you learn those shared…

  2. Adult CPR (Skill I) 30 min

    When a person’s heart stops, they fall down, stop breathing normally and have no pulse. CPR pushes blood to the brain until help comes. You do not have to be a doctor to do CPR. Skill I shows the judge how you do CPR by…

  3. Adult CPR with an AED (Skill II) 30 min

    An AED is a small machine that can shock a stopped heart back into a normal rhythm. It talks to you and tells you what to do. Anyone can use one. Skill II is like Skill I, but an AED arrives while you are doing CPR, and…

Unit 2 · Infant CPR and choking

Skill III (infant CPR) and Skill VI (choking).

  1. Infant CPR (Skill III) 30 min

    An infant is a baby younger than 1 year old. Babies are small, so CPR is gentler. You use fingers or thumbs, smaller breaths and a baby-size mask. In Skill III you are alone, so you do CPR for 2 minutes before you call…

  2. Choking (Skill VI) 30 min

    Food or a small object can get stuck in the throat and block air. A person who is choking badly cannot talk, cough or breathe. Back blows and belly pushes can get the object out. Skill VI is short—only 3 minutes—so you…

Unit 3 · Injuries

Skill V (severe bleeding and shock), Skill VII (open fracture and splint) and Skill IX (severe burn).

  1. Severe bleeding and shock (Skill V) 30 min

    A deep cut on an arm or leg can bleed so fast that a person could die before an ambulance comes. Pressing hard on the wound and using a tourniquet can stop the bleeding. Skill V gives you 5 minutes to stop bleeding and…

  2. Open fracture and splinting (Skill VII) 35 min

    A fracture is a broken bone. In an open fracture, the broken bone breaks through the skin. It hurts a lot and can get infected. A splint keeps the bone from moving so it does not get worse. Skill VII gives you 6 minutes…

  3. Severe burns (Skill IX) 30 min

    Burns can come from fire, hot water, hot stoves, chemicals or electricity. A bad burn hurts the skin deeply and can cause shock. Cooling the burn fast and covering it gently are the most important first aid steps. Skill…

Unit 4 · Heat, allergies and overdose

Skill VIII (heat emergency), Skill IV (EpiPen) and Skill X (naloxone).

  1. Heat emergencies (Skill VIII) 30 min

  2. Allergic reactions and opioid overdose: EpiPen and naloxone (Skills IV and X) 30 min

    Some people have allergies so strong that their throat swells shut. An EpiPen gives medicine that can save their life. Other people stop breathing because of opioid drugs. Naloxone nasal spray can wake them up and help…
